newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: QUEENSLAND PLANE CRASH SURVIVORS STABLE
Five survivors of a plane crash in the sea in far north Queensland
last night are in a stable condition in the Cairns Base Hospital
hospital this morning.
All five people on board the twin-engined Piper Aztec were rescued after it ditched into the ocean while en-route from Horn Island to
Cairns.
A rescue helicopter spotted the passengers in the sea just off
Double Island.
The helicopter winched four of them to safety while a rescue boat from Cairns airport picked up the fifth.
Cairns police say all five were taken to hospital for observation
but they believe none was seriously injured.
GOVERNMENT THINK TANK ON SIMPSON DESERT
The future of the Simpson Desert will be in the spotlight today.
Queensland, South Australian and Northern Territory Governments
will meet in Alice Springs to address what's being described as the
desert's deteriorating state.
One of the key issues will be the management of introduced animals, which are being blamed for the rapid extinction of native fauna.
Authorities are also concerned about the safety of people crossing
the Simpson, and will discuss emergency response procedures to get
to people who get into difficulties.
EUTHANASIA DEBATE CONTINUES..
The son of the first person to use the Northern Territory's
voluntary euthanasia law says parliament's decision shouldn't be at
the cost of the terminally ill and their families.
Rod Dent says it's clear debate will be based on religion and
morals, but the human cost of over-riding the law must also be taken into account.
Debate on a private member's bill to over-turn the euthanasia law
resumes in a side chamber of Federal Parliament on Wednesday, after
it was suspended last week in uproar.
Meanwhile, the AMA says the current debate has been clouded with
confusion about what actually constitutes euthanasia.
PUSH FOR ALTERNATIVE ENERGY CARS
Australian car manufacturers are being urged to spend more on
research, to find an alternative to petrol-driven vehicles.
More than 100 world experts on electric and solar cars are in Adelaide for a two-day conference.
Organiser, Di Sullivan, says as the world begins to experience an
oil shortage, vehicles will need to be powered by another resource.
And, she's worried that industry isn't allowing itself enough time
to develop new technologies.
MORE ALLEGATIONS AGAINST QUEENSLAND POLICE MINISTER COOPER
Queensland's Corrective Services Minister Russell Cooper is again
being forced to defend his reputation.
The Federated Clerks Union says it has evidence of an alleged deal in which Mr Cooper and National Party operative, Matthew Heery
pressured prison officers to continue a strike in return for a wish
list.
Mr Cooper denies he made the deal in the lead up to the crucial
Mundingburra by-election.
The Criminal Justice Commission is already examining a secret
pre-election deal involving Mr Cooper, the then-Opposition leader
Rob Borbidge and the Police Union.
The Opposition says the Premier should consider whether Mr Cooper
should stand aside while the CJC investigates the matter.
Meanwhile, the CJC can't confirm or deny if it's received any
evidence from the Clerk's union dealing with the allegations about
Mr Cooper.
RESCUERS' HOPES NOT HIGH IN BOAT SEARCH
Police have resumed a search, with little hope of finding three
men, missing in a boat off Port Campbell in south west Victoria.
There have been no confirmed sightings of the men who failed to
return on Saturday.
Water Police say the men weren't equipped for two nights at sea and are fearing the worst at the beginning of this morning's extensive
search.
The police helicopter is sweeping the coastline while a fixed wing
aircraft is searching offshore.
COCKROACH BOMBS POSSIBLE FIRE HAZARD
Queensland's Emergency Services Minister Mick Veivers, has warned
domestic devices designed to kill cockroaches and other household
pests could be a fire risk.
Investigations have found a recent house fire on the Gold Coast was
believed to have been started because the home's power was not switched off when a pest bomb was activated.
Mr Veivers is urging people to read the instructions of pest bombs
carefully.
He says although it doesn't appear to be a major problem, the
likelihood of a fire sparked by a cockroach bomb going undetected is high, because most people leave their homes after setting off
the devices.
CONCERNS ABOUT LEGAL IMPLICATIONS OF GENETIC TESTING
New South Wale's young lawyers have raised concerns about the
potential dangers of genetic testing in Australia.
Young Lawyers President, Brett Boon, says genetic testing is being
used by insurance companies and employers in the United States to
screen out people whose genes indicate they're at a higher risk of
developing serious diseases.
Mr Boon says the federal government needs to bring in laws to
address possible discrimination, based on genetic testing.
ARKELL SEEKING TO ADDRESS HIS CRITIC
The former Illawarra MP named in New South Wales parliament last
week during a debate on paedophilia, says he'd welcome the
opportunity to address the State's Upper House.
Labor backbencher Franca Arena named retired Supreme Court judge David Yeldham QC and former MP Frank Arkell.
Ms Arena was condemned by Premier Bob Carr for abusing
parliamentary privelege.
The Government is now seeking to change Upper House standing orders
to allow citizens the right of reply to accusations made by MPs in
the Legislative Council.
LINK TO MENOPAUSE PROBLEMS AND FULL TIME WORK
A study of middle aged women has found their health improves if
they give up full-time work.
Professor Lorraine Dennerstein, of the University of Melbourne, says previous studies have shown women are healthier if they are in
paid work, but those studies have focussed on young women.
She's released her findings at the International Congress on the
Menopause being held in Sydney this week.
Professor Dennerstein says she found the health of middle-aged women improved if they reduced the number of hours they were
working.
BISHOP CALLS FOR STATEMENT AGAINST RACISM
A church leader has challenged the Prime Minister to spell out his
stance on a tolerant, multicultural society, at this morning's annual prayer breakfast.
The Anglican Archbishop of Canberra, George Browning, saysAustralia
seems to be backing out of the debate on immigration for fear of
losing its place in the region.
He told 500 churchgoers and MPs at a Parliament House service last night that Australia was afraid of losing visitors and trade, and
it was a shame moral issues came down to economics.
Bishop Browning says as Martin Luther King had a dream, so
Aboriginal people have a dream of reconciliation.
He says Australia won't come of age until that's achieved.
CORONIAL INQUEST INTO PNG ASSASSINATION
Papua New Guinea's Prime Minister, Sir Julius Chan, says a retired
Sri Lankan judge will seek out the full truth behind last month's
assassination of the Premier of Bougainville.
The Judge has been nominated by the Secretary General of the inquiry, following a request from Sir Julius.
The Papua New Guinea military and Bougainville rebels have accused
each other of murdering the Bougainville Premier, Theodore Miriung.
He was shot in front of his wife and children in south west Bougainville last month.
